Luis’s last message says it was Ray who called him over to the container; the cell tower puts them both in the same place. After the death, at 02.09, the forklift was logged into with his card, and at 02.12 the rack was toppled with the forks.
The union rep was at dock 7 at the time; she was the one Luis trusted.
Three thousand dollars. We fought, last week. But I wouldn’t kill my brother. I’ve got a tag on my ankle; I can’t leave the house after 22.00.

The rack in aisle 14:

· Four anchor bolts snapped; the fracture surfaces bright and fresh, no sign of fatigue. The bolts were snapped by being pushed from the side, at floor level.
· At the foot of the rack upright, two parallel forklift fork scrape marks; the paint is forklift 3’s yellow.
· The rack’s load was under the limit. It could not have fallen on its own.
Warehouse procedures are the company’s business; I run the shift.

My card… He saw the crates; one phone call and it’s all over, the job’s over. We talked by the container, with the crowbar; he said ‘bube’. Then… I toppled the rack, with the forklift. So it would look like an accident.
Luis’s messages. Everybody talks about everybody.
In the office, writing the shift report. I heard the noise and ran. Luis was tired, he hit the rack with the forklift, that’s all. I warned him how many times.
He rubs the back of his neck.

My inspection report goes out through official channels.

I’ve been looking at racks for thirty years. This one didn’t fatigue; it was pushed over. Someone set a forklift’s forks against the foot of the upright and snapped the bolts from the side. Only someone who knows how to drive a forklift does that.
He pushes his glasses up his nose.
Can a rack fall on its own?

On the night of 12 July 2030, at the Lakeshore Freight warehouse in Pilsen, Chicago, forklift operator Luis Ortega (29) was found dead under a pallet rack that toppled in aisle 14.

The shift supervisor reported it at 02.20 as a workplace accident. In the warehouse on the night shift: shift supervisor Ray Kowalski, inventory clerk Marisol Reyes, security guard Dwayne Carter, union rep Teresa Novak. City workplace safety inspector Pete Lindqvist arrived in the morning.
Request the city’s workplace safety inspection report
Shipping lists come to me; I don’t know beyond that.

The crates. The ones from Paris. They were sticking ‘machine parts’ labels on them, with auction numbers underneath. They’re listed as machine parts in my inventory too. Luis said, ‘I’m going to tell someone about this.’
She folds her arms across her chest and lifts her chin.
What was Luis talking about these last days?
On the 01.30 break. He was typing something on his phone. Then I went back to the office, to the inventory count.
When did you last see him that night?

Night shift, 12 July:

· Luis Ortega — dock 4, forklift 3
· Teresa Novak — dock 7
· Marisol Reyes — inventory office
· Ray Kowalski — shift supervisor; note: ‘special shipment, container 22’

Container 22: sender Maison Delorme, Paris. Declared as: machine parts.

The autopsy showed the blow to the head was struck in life and the crushing came after death; the inspection showed the bolts were snapped by pushing. The operations line gave the card in the forklift, the phone line the last messages. The parole line only cleared the brother.
You can open two lines. Before you open one, think about which will change the answer.

Shift supervisor Ray Kowalski was relabelling the auction crates from Paris as ‘machine parts’. When forklift operator Luis Ortega took photos and wrote that he would go to the union, Kowalski called him over to the container and killed him with a crowbar. Twenty minutes later he got into the forklift with his own card, snapped the rack’s bolts with the forks and toppled the rack onto the body.

Card and sensor log of forklift 3:

· 01.12–01.48 on Luis Ortega’s card, at dock 4.
· 02.09 logged in: SUP-01 — Ray Kowalski.
· 02.11 fork height 6 cm, forward pressure; 02.12 sudden loss of load.
· 02.13 logged out; the forklift reverses out of aisle 14.

· 01.31 → Teresa Novak: ‘Ray is changing the labels on the Paris crates. Container 22. I took photos. Coming to the union in the morning, I need a lawyer.’
· 01.44 → Marisol Reyes: ‘Ray called me over to the container. If anything happens, the photos are in the cloud.’
· The photos in the cloud: double-labelled crates; one with a Paris auction lot number.

The four bolts fixing the rack to the floor; the fracture surfaces bright, freshly snapped.
